title: I Also Sent My Children to a Nonselective, Overwhelmingly Minority Public School, but It Wasn’t a Sacrifice. -wasnt-a-sacrifice/
author: Eva Moskowitz
summary: Eva Moskowitz, founder of the Success Academy charter network, responds to Nikole Hannah-Jones's essay by telling her own story of enrolling her children in the nonselective, overwhelmingly Black and Latino Harlem schools she had just founded. She acknowledges the social costs her daughter in particular felt, but argues that unlike Najya Hannah-Jones her children did not sacrifice their education. Moskowitz agrees that educational failure falls hardest on poor Black and Latino communities, yet insists that segregation is not an adequate explanation for the institutional failures Hannah-Jones describes. Her evidence is Success Academy's results, including proficiency and Level 4 rates far above district schools, entire schools scoring Level 4, and extensive AP passing among lottery-admitted, largely low-income students. She concludes that no child should absorb inadequate instruction so adults can show solidarity, and urges families to consider strong charter schools.
points: Moskowitz argues Najya did not need more white classmates; she needed a teacher who checked her math work.
She contends that even celebrated district schools like Stuyvesant are constrained by a system that rewards compliance and defines rigor downward.
At Success Academy Bronx 4, where 83 percent of students are economically disadvantaged, all 195 test takers earned Level 4.
Success substitutes externally scored AP exams for Regents exams in high school so that grades cannot mask a lack of mastery.
She rejects the moral argument that privileged parents must keep their children in weak schools as an act of solidarity.
quotes: When Nikole Hannah-Jones writes that her daughter finally told her, “Sometimes I wish instead of always thinking about other kids, you would have thought about me,” every parent who works in education should stop and sit with those words.
Both children remained at Success Academy through high school. Here my story diverges from Hannah-Jones’s: I do not believe I sacrificed their education.

These are not small imperfections in an otherwise sound system. They are institutional failures: failures of curriculum, teaching, assessment, classroom management, grading, leadership and basic adult responsibility.
But segregation is not an adequate explanation for educational failure. And integration, however desirable for other reasons, will not solve the profound problems of our educational system.
Hannah-Jones’s daughter did not need more white classmates to have her math work checked. She needed a teacher who checked it. She needed honest assessment, so that an A represented mastery.
Externally scored and nationally comparable, AP exams make it harder for schools to mistake reassuring grades for mastery.

No child should be required to absorb years of inadequate instruction so that adults can demonstrate solidarity. The goal of education policy cannot be to persuade families with options to tolerate failure alongside families without them.
I wasn’t trying to sacrifice my child to a greater cause. I was trying to build schools where nobody’s child had to be sacrificed.
